institutionName: Institut d'études politiques de Paris (Sciences Po)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The fact that the destination had courses in English, which would also be able to be pre-approved by University of Copenhagen (UCPH). Since I went on exchange during the 5th semester of my bachelor, finding courses that could substitute Dansk og Komparativ Politik 3 and Europæisk politik wasn't easy. Also, I love France and the French language, so I saw this as an opportunity to improve my French language skills and get a French perspective on politics.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The welcome program was online due to Covid so it was not too informing, but the Premiere Cycle Echange people are really good at answering any questions via email (unless they're on vacation, which they were almost all of August).

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Not a lot. I had to seek information and guidance on my own most of the time.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It is almost more difficult to find affordable housing in Paris than in Copenhagen. I ended up on Airbnb and found a small studio that wasn't too expensive. I didn't get into the Cité Universitaire, so I was pretty much on my own. My recommendation is to start looking early, and be prepared to spend at least 800 euros/month on a very very small studio.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It is expensive and difficult to find a place close to the university. Sciences Po doesn't have any student housing - they refer to the Cité. It is also a great experience not living in the Cité and finding a place on your own. I lived closer to the centre of Paris, and it felt very "authentic".

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The administration sends out the final course catalogue and a guide for the registration. The registration opens (usually at around 16h and closes some time next day). Throughout the course registration period, some students will drop courses, so if you don't get your first priorities right away, keep checking throughout the registration period because spots might open up. 

It was very stressful, especially because I needed to register for certain courses that would substitute the obligatory courses I was supposed to have back home at UCPH. I suggest being in touch with the Premier Cycle Echange people weeks in advance. They should send you the list of courses that they expect to offer when you're going on exchange, however, the course list can be subject to change (as late as days before the registration). This happened to me. One of my “obligatory” courses were suddenly not on the course list, so I had to find a new course and send a new pre-approval application to UCPH (who were on vacation and didn't approve it until the first week of August - and by that time Sciences Po had gone on vacation). The course registration is open for about 24 hours and I definitely suggest sitting ready when the registration opens because the courses are filling up fast. I also suggest preparing a list of at least 5 other courses, that you can choose if your first priorities are filled up.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Again, the Premier Cycle Echange people were ready to answer any question I had about course registration. But they don't answer any questions during the registration period - during the registration, you're on your own.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: After the whole situation with the course, that suddenly wasn't on the course list, and after finding a new course to substitute that, I got all my first priority-courses. I was also ready by the computer when the registration opened, which I think is the best advice I can give anyone who is going to Sciences Po. Also, use the search function on your computer to search for your courses on the list, because there are a lot of courses.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Prepare a list of courses, be ready when the registration opens, prepare yourself for the possibility that you wont get all the courses you want, and finally, be prepared to send more than one pre-approval to UCPH.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses at Sciences Po were a lot more practical than theoretical, compared to the courses at UCPH. There was a lot more work at Sciences Po throughout the semester and the type of assignments varied a lot - I had to do presentations, research papers, essays, handwritten exams, news analysis etc. A big recommendation is to start on your assignment as early as possible because by the end of the semester there is a lot of work to do, and it can be very stressful the last couple of weeks.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching varied from course to course. In some courses the teaching style was more based on class discussion, whereas in other courses the teacher spoke for 2 hours and then the students just listened and took notes. There is really no way you can know what teaching style each teacher has until you take the course (course description doesn't say).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
European Integration and its Challenges (5 ECTS) - was approved by UCPH as Europæisk Politik
The Decision-Making Process of the European Union - an Insider's View (5 ECTS) - was approved by UCPH as Europæisk Politik
Comparative Politics (10 ECTS) - was approved by UCPH as Dansk og Komparativ Politik 3
Citizen Politics and Democracy in Times of Crisis (5 ECTS)
International Conflicts (5 ECTS)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I can definitely recommend International Conflicts with Jean-Yves Haine. Even though it's mostly him that talks during the class, he is so knowledgeable about the subject and I found that the 2 hours ran by. If you like IR like me, then you will love this course.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The coffee - a latte usually costs 4,5 or 5 euros. Most things in Paris are expensive - especially the cafés and restaurants near Sciences Po. However, it is (usually) cheaper to eat at restaurants than in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Sciences Po has a lot of athletic and cultural activities that you can even get ECTS for - I however wasn't able to join any, because I could register for max 30 ECTS, and all my ECTS had to be related to political science courses. A lot of the other exchange students from other countries participated in these activities, but they could also choose more freely from the courses.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I didn't partake in any, unfortunately.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The museums, the monuments, take a walk along the Seine - or really anywhere in Paris. Walking is the best was to see and discover new places. The Louis Vuitton Foundation had a great exhibition when I was in Paris. L'Orangerie (free if you're under 26 but you need to book a ticket in advance) and Musée d'Orsay (free if you're under 26) is also great museums and a lot smaller than Louvre (also free) , so you can see all of it in one day.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy - people are very nice and the other exchange students are also very eager to get to know you, so as long as you're open to talk to new people, you'll be fine. The international students and the “local” students at Sciences Po doesn't really socialize with each other though - there's very much “two communities”.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: In terms of socializing with the other international students, just strike up a conversation with the person sitting next to you in class. Don't be afraid to talk to the people in your class, because almost everyone is just like you and doesn't have any friends yet. In terms of the local students, I don't really have the answer to that, other than to take courses in French. All the courses in English are mostly filled with international exchange students, while the courses in French are mostly filled with local Sciences Po students. You can also get a “buddy” when you arrive (a buddy is a local Sciences Po student, but I haven't had one myself).

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Many local French people don't speak English. Knowing a little French can get you a long way.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: (Most of) the people are really nice and helpful.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. The process isn't as easy as UCPH makes it seem. The most challenging thing for me was getting my courses pre-approved and finding courses that could potentially get pre-approved. Even though the process is long, stressful and difficult, I highly recommend going. It is so worth it. Looking back, all the challenges only made me stronger. 

2. Be prepared for a lot of work. It is not going to be 4 months vacation - if anything it's going to be the hardest (but best semester) of your bachelor. Start on your assignments as soon as possible, but remember to enjoy the city and your stay (you only need to pass)

3. Be open. If you have that approach, you will make friends easier, do more things out of your comfort zone and develop, both academically and socially.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: There is a lot of information on Sciences Po's website, but it can be a bit difficult to find. Write to Premier Cycle Echange for any questions.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting amazing people, exploring Paris and trying a whole new way of studying at university.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Balancing studying and free time.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
